Viewforth investment memo · VAR-NO

Var Energi: a sound business priced as an exceptional one, at the top of its valuation range while its earnings per share fall on every price path

13 November 2026. Share price NOK 49.6 (11 November 2026), equal to USD 5.20 at NOK 9.54 per USD. All amounts are in USD unless stated otherwise.

Var Energi is a sound business priced as an exceptional one.

At NOK 49.6 the shares do not offer what Richard looks for, which is fundamental outcomes and odds of upgrades that are unusually skewed to the positive. A share price in the low-to-mid NOK 30s would offer it.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions on the business and its investment case

The business. Var Energi is the third-largest producer on the Norwegian continental shelf. It will produce about 386,000 barrels of oil equivalent (boe) a day in 2026 and about 428,000 in 2027, once BlueNord's Danish barrels are added; two-thirds is liquids and one-third gas. Var sells a commodity at the market price, pays 78% tax on the marginal dollar of profit and distributes USD 350-400m a quarter. Eni owns 63% of the shares, falling to 57% after the BlueNord acquisition. Var is a well-financed, competently led, mid-ranked operator in a good basin.

The investment case at NOK 49.6. A buyer at NOK 49.6 pays 14.0 times earnings two years out, the top of the stock's listed history, for EPS that the model has falling from USD 0.78 in 2026 to 0.51 in 2027 and 0.34 in 2028. In return the buyer receives a cash yield of about 10%, which free cash flow covers in 2026 and 2027 and does not cover in 2028. At the guideline fair multiple of 9.41x, the model's total shareholder return is -26.4% to March 2028 and -20.5% to September 2029.

The seven things that matter most

  1. The oil and gas price sets the level of Var's EPS, but the shape of the EPS path is close to fixed. The realised oil and gas price explains about three-quarters of the fall in EPS from 2026 to 2028, and it can put 2027 EPS anywhere from USD 0.27 to 0.81. On all three price paths, EPS does not grow in 2027 and falls in 2028. Everything the company itself controls is worth only a few cents a share.
  2. Viewforth's operating forecasts are above the Street's; Viewforth's per-share forecasts are below them. For 2027 our revenue and EBITDA are about 6% above consensus, our net income is in line and our EPS is 14% below. The EPS gap comes from the share count, the hybrid coupons and finance costs. Consensus EPS therefore has to fall from early 2027 even if the business performs exactly as we expect. The year of rising estimates that carried the shares will end for reasons unrelated to trading.
  3. The dividend is uncovered in 2028 without any bear case. Norwegian petroleum tax on a strong year is paid in the first half of the following year, so a strong 2027 costs Var cash in 2028. Distributions exceed free cash flow in 2028 on every price path; the paths differ only in whether cash banked in 2026-27 or new debt fills the gap. The balance sheet can carry the 2028 gap on every path.
  4. The multiple the market pays in 2028 is a vote on whether it believes the dividend. At the guideline multiple the shares would stand near NOK 30 in March 2028, where today's dividend would yield 16%. The market has priced Var on such a yield before: the yield peaked at 18% in early 2023, when the dividend was funded by borrowing, and today's yield is the lowest since the 2022 listing. If investors believe the dividend through 2028, 11-13x is the more likely resting multiple. The memo's 18-month horizon ends in spring 2028, the moment of greatest doubt about the dividend.
  5. The favourable surprises are near, and they concern cash rather than earnings. Winter gas prices, a fourth-quarter volume recovery, 2027 free cash flow well above consensus and the dividend framework due on 9 February 2027 can each support the shares over the next three months. None of these events raises EPS two years out. From the second quarter of 2027 the dated events turn against the shares.
  6. Var's share price embeds the optimistic commodity view more fully than its peers' share prices do. Var trades at the 99th percentile of its own valuation history, while Aker BP, whose cash flow rises into 2027-28, trades at the 43rd. The sector's re-rating explains about half of Var's premium to its own median multiple. The other half is specific to Var, and Var did not earn it through operating delivery.
  7. Three developments would turn Var into the kind of investment Richard looks for. The first is a share price in the low-to-mid NOK 30s, where a held dividend yields 13-15% and the return at the guideline multiple turns positive. The second is evidence that the price deck is structurally higher: TTF gas (the Dutch Title Transfer Facility benchmark) above EUR 60/MWh through the 2027 storage-refill season, and 2028-29 consensus still rising after the per-share correction. The third is two quarters of delivery in the top half of a 2027 production guide set near 440,000 boe a day.
The largest driver of the return is the multiple the market pays in spring 2028. Each turn of that multiple moves the share price by NOK 3.2, and the dividend's credibility decides whether the multiple settles nearer 8x or 12x.

The five judgements that move the value most, with the arithmetic

Judgement 1: the price deck. The base deck has a realised price of USD 87/boe in 2027 (Brent USD 81 a barrel, TTF EUR 51.5/MWh) and USD 71/boe in 2028 (Brent USD 72, TTF EUR 35/MWh).

  • Production of 428,000 boe a day for 365 days is 156m boe, so each USD 10/boe of realised price is USD 1.56bn of revenue.
  • Var pays no royalties and its cost base does not move with price, so the whole USD 1.56bn also reaches EBITDA and pre-tax profit.
  • After 79% tax, the USD 1.56bn becomes USD 0.33bn of net income. Over 2,744.8m shares that is about USD 0.12 of EPS (the model's own figure is 0.117), equal to 23% of 2027 EPS and 34% of 2028 EPS.
  • About half the tax on a year's profit is paid in that year. USD 0.95bn of a USD 10/boe price move therefore reaches free cash flow in the year of the move, and USD 0.6bn of that USD 0.95bn goes back in tax in the first half of the following year (my arithmetic).
  • A USD 10/boe move is roughly USD 8 a barrel on Brent and EUR 8/MWh on TTF moving together (my arithmetic on the 65/35 liquids-to-gas mix). A plausible error in the price deck is two to two-and-a-half times that size. On the bear deck (Brent 65, TTF 35) 2027 EPS is about USD 0.27; on the bull deck (Brent 95, TTF 75) it is about USD 0.81. I weight the bear, base and bull decks at 30, 50 and 20 in 100, which gives a probability-weighted 2027 EPS of USD 0.50.

Judgement 2: the dividend is held at USD 350m a quarter through 2028.

  • On the base deck, 2028 free cash flow of USD 665m, less USD 110m of hybrid coupons, leaves USD 555m against dividends of USD 1,400m: a gap of USD 845m.
  • Surpluses after distributions of USD 2,165m in 2026 and USD 260m in 2027 pre-fund the 2028 gap. Net interest-bearing debt rises from about USD 2.3bn at end-2026 to USD 4.1bn at end-2028. That is 0.45x EBITDA, or 0.65x with the hybrids counted as debt, against a ceiling of 1.3x.
  • If the deck is USD 10/boe lower in both 2027 and 2028, free cash flow is USD 0.95bn lower in 2027 and USD 0.34bn lower in 2028 (the USD 0.95bn less the USD 0.61bn of tax no longer due). Net debt then ends 2028 near USD 5.4bn on EBITDA of USD 7.4bn: 0.72x, or 0.96x with hybrids (my arithmetic). The dividend still holds.
  • Only the full bear deck takes net debt to about USD 6bn and 1.1x. On the bear deck I expect a fall-back to the stated policy of paying 25-30% of post-tax operating cash flow, which is USD 0.95-1.15bn a year. That is a cut of 20-30%, taking the dividend per share from USD 0.51 to 0.35-0.42. I put the probability of a cut within 18 months at about 15 in 100.

Judgement 3: the multiple the market pays in spring 2028. Two-year-forward EPS in the model's March 2028 column is about USD 0.333.

  • Each turn of multiple is therefore worth USD 0.33 a share, NOK 3.2, or 6.4% of today's share price.
  • At the guideline 9.41x the share price is NOK 29.9. Adding NOK 6.5 of dividends gives NOK 36.5, a return of -26%.
  • If investors believe the dividend and ask a 12-14% yield on the USD 0.51 dividend, the share price is NOK 35-41. That is 11-13x, and a return of -17% to -5%.
  • If the multiple stays at 14.0x, the return is +3%: the dividend merely offsets the fall in earnings.
  • If the sector's re-rating fades as well, taking Var to its own 75th percentile (8.1x) or median (6.9x), the return is -35% or -43%.
  • To break even at 9.41x, forward EPS must reach USD 0.48. That requires a realised price about USD 12.5/boe above our 2029-30 deck, roughly Brent USD 82 and TTF EUR 41/MWh sustained (my arithmetic).

Judgement 4: the per-share basis of consensus. Consensus EPS still divides net income by the pre-merger share count and ignores the hybrid coupons. For 2028, consensus net income divided by the 2,496.4m pre-merger shares reproduces the consensus EPS figure almost exactly. On the post-merger basis of 2,744.8m shares, after USD 110m of coupons, consensus EPS is materially lower.

  • Some brokers already use the correct basis, so my central estimate of the mechanical fall in the consensus median is 5% for 2027 and 10% for 2028.
  • The correction has two consequences. Revisions turn negative without any change in the business, and the true multiple is 14x, not the 11.5-12.8x shown on screens.
  • If I am wrong and brokers have already re-based their models, our EPS is unchanged and one source of negative estimate momentum disappears.

Judgement 5: volumes, plateau or decline. Our base case is 385,000 boe a day standalone plus 43,000 from BlueNord in 2027. The company's target is about 450,000. DNB Carnegie has standalone production falling to 346,000 by 2028, against our 382,000.

  • A marginal barrel earns the price less variable cost less depreciation: USD 71 - 3 - 24 = USD 44/boe of EBIT at the 2028 deck.
  • 10,000 boe a day is 3.65m boe a year. At USD 44/boe that is USD 0.16bn of EBIT, USD 0.035bn of net income and USD 0.013 of EPS.
  • If the company meets its target (+22,000 boe a day), EPS rises by USD 0.03. If DNB Carnegie is right (-36,000 boe a day in 2028), revenue falls by USD 0.9bn, EBIT by USD 0.58bn, net income by USD 0.125bn and EPS by USD 0.046 (14% of 2028 EPS), and free cash flow falls by about USD 0.2bn a year.
  • Volume is therefore worth less than a USD 4/boe move in price. Volume matters because it decides which story the market tells about Var: "plateau and yield" or "decline and cut".

GradesScorecard of the twelve topics

#1Strong/improving tailwinds in the operating environment; and an absence of headwinds/risks

Conclusion: The external tailwinds are strong, but they form a supply-shock peak that has begun to turn, with a dated cluster of headwinds in 2027-28. This topic offers Var support for two quarters and no absence of headwinds.

Evidence. Oil and gas prices are high because supply is short, not because demand is growing. The supports for the price are near-term and cyclical. The headwinds are structural, and most of them carry dates in 2027-28.

Inference. The current price environment is a supply-shock peak. The tailwinds are strong, cyclical and visible for one or two winters; the headwinds are slower, structural and clustered in 2027-28.

The trend turned on 22 October, when Brent peaked. The first step of price normalisation is therefore arriving about a quarter earlier than the base case assumed. For that reason I weight the bear path at 30 in 100 and the bull path at 20 (the previous round of analysis had 20 and 25), while leaving the base deck unchanged.

So what. The environment supports Var in the first half of 2027 and works against it in 2028. The combination that hurts Var most is a lower commodity price with a firm krone, and that is the combination the forecasters expect.

Strongest counter-case. The gas market may stay short for longer than any price deck assumes. DNB Carnegie (10 November, as summarised by AlphaSense, so indicative only) puts the 2027 TTF curve near USD 23/mmbtu, against a broker consensus of USD 17 that matches our deck. If the curve were delivered, the extra USD 6/mmbtu would be worth about USD 35 per boe of gas, USD 12 per boe across Var's mix and USD 0.14 of EPS, lifting 2027 EPS to about USD 0.65 (my arithmetic).

Two facts temper this counter-case. Spot gas ended the winter 10-60% below the forward curve in three of the last five winters. And the same DNB Carnegie note calculates that Var's share price already implies gas at about USD 22.5/mmbtu, against USD 14-16 for Aker BP and Equinor.

What would change my view. TTF gas above EUR 60/MWh through the 2027 storage-refill season; delays to the 2027-28 LNG start-ups; Brent holding above USD 85 after the Hormuz premium has gone.

Against the market. I agree with consensus that prices normalise: consensus revenue falls 10% in 2027 and 16% in 2028. I disagree with the narrative that Europe's need for Norwegian gas supports the gas price. Europe's need supports Var's volumes and contract values, while LNG sets the marginal price.

Score: 20, set by the Rater. The tailwind is a supply-shock peak already turning: Brent fell from USD 111 to 91.5, the North Sea crude premium collapsed, European gas demand is 16% below its 2017-21 level, and 40-50m tonnes a year of new LNG with start dates arrive in 2027-28, while costs are rising (rigs, subsea) and the krone is firm on 70% of opex; winter gas and the Russian LNG ban support only one or two quarters. Consensus sales growth at the 0.5th percentile (-16.9%) tells the truth here, so the net external force is clearly negative over two to three years, a little worse than BP's oil normalisation because gas and cost headwinds are dated on top, though not the contracted supply collapse of Maersk; coherent with the External change forces group (22).

#2Strong/improving internally-driven corporate change forces; and an absence of problems/risks

Conclusion: Internal change at Var is broad and well funded, but its earnings pay-off is spent and it now comes with visible operating slippage. Internal change therefore supports the dividend without creating earnings upgrades.

Evidence. The positive changes are real and well resourced, and they sit in what management decides. The strategy has moved from building to harvesting: tie-backs around owned hubs, capex held near USD 2.5bn a year for 2027-32, and a first step outside Norway through BlueNord. Var bought BlueNord largely with its own shares, valued at about 1.6x net asset value, for assets valued at about 1.25x: a smart use of expensive paper.

The negative changes are recent, and they sit in operations. The one identified cost step, retiring the old Balder production unit in 2028 (a saving of USD 117m a year net to Var), depends on compressor work at Jotun that has slipped to "2027 or 2028". I put the probability of retirement in 2028 at 55 in 100.

Inference. The change that re-rated the shares has fully worked through and been paid for: a new chief executive in 2023, production doubled and debt cut. The 2026 changes add reserve life, gas and payout; they do not add EPS. BlueNord brings about 11% more volume for 10% more shares, which lifts EPS by only 1-3%, and its synergies are worth about USD 0.016 a share a year.

Management raises what it controls through capital allocation and under-delivers on what it controls through operations. The delivery now required is also of a different kind: not two very large projects and an acquisition, but more than 50 wells and about eight project sanctions every year. Var has shown that kind of competence for only one year.

So what. Corporate change underwrites the production plateau and the dividend, but it is not a source of earnings upgrades. The only company-made upside left lies in strengths Var has yet to demonstrate, namely 95% operated uptime and unit cost back at USD 10/boe, and together those two strengths are worth USD 0.03-0.04 a share.

Strongest counter-case. The chief executive does deals well, and another deal is plausible, at about 30 in 100 within 18 months. The small projects of 2026 came in on time, lead times for selected subsea equipment have fallen from 30 to 18 months, and he bought shares in August 2026 at NOK 48.55. A cash-funded, Neptune-style acquisition would add to EPS in a way that the share-funded BlueNord deal does not.

What would change my view. Two consecutive quarters of operated production efficiency at 95% or better; sanction of the Balder retirement with the full-year results; a transaction that adds to EPS, not only to barrels.

Against the market. Investors were positive on BlueNord (Morgan Stanley's investor feedback in September), and the Street, apart from DNB Carnegie, accepts the 450,000 boe a day plateau. I agree that the BlueNord deal is sensible. I differ on two points that no broker has written down: the deal is neutral per share, and the plateau requires a capability Var has shown for only one year.

Score: 47, set by the Rater. The company's own moves are real and funded (BlueNord as a first step outside Norway, the harvest strategy with capex held near USD 2.5bn, Neptune synergies of USD 600m against 300m, dividend raised twice) but they add reserve life and payout, not earnings per share (BlueNord adds 1-3% to EPS for 10% more shares), and they are offset by internal problems: operated efficiency down from 97% to 91%, scheduled reserves for 2026-29 down from 527m to 438m boe unexplained, and the Balder retirement saving at only 55 in 100 for 2028. Real dated positives offset by present problems sit just below 50, a shade above the Internal change forces group (45) because the BlueNord move and the synergy record are genuine, between Hexatronic and Indus.

#3A value chain and industry structure that is favourable; a business model with competitive advantage and barriers to entry; an above average or better financial profile; a dynamic management team with stretching goals, the right strategy and winning culture

Conclusion: The industry structure and fiscal regime are favourable and widely shared, while Var's own advantage, financial profile and operating culture are average. Var's foundations are therefore sound without being distinctive.

Evidence. Industry structure. The Norwegian shelf has consolidated from 56 active companies to 25. Peers co-operate through joint exploration and licence swaps, barriers to entry are high, and the state co-invests through the tax system. But the oil and gas price is set outside the basin, and suppliers hold the upper hand: there are only three subsea contractors and 22 suitable rigs.

Competitive advantage. Var's own edge is hub incumbency: tie-backs to its existing hubs break even at about USD 30/boe and earn returns of about 35%. Against that edge, Var ranks third on cost, earns lower returns than Aker BP in the same tax regime, and has a production base that declines about twice as fast as the norm.

Financial profile. EBITDA margins above 80% become a net margin of about 14% after tax, even in the peak year. Ordinary equity is close to nil: of about USD 1.9bn of book equity, USD 1.75bn is hybrid capital.

Management. Chief executive Nick Walker's record on transactions, funding and payouts is strong. On in-year operations, volumes and costs have landed at or below the bottom of his guidance two years running. Eni appoints a third of the board, buys about 79% of Var's output and needs the cash, which reliably produces dividends and reliably rules out buybacks.

Inference. Most of Var's advantages belong to the basin and are shared with every producer on it. The industry structure protects access to licences and to cheap debt; it does not protect margins.

One finding cuts the other way and deserves emphasis: the build-out did not damage the economics of Var's barrel. At a like-for-like price the business earns what it earned before, so the per-share disappointment sits wholly below EBIT.

So what. These foundations justify modelling stable volumes, a low cost of debt and a defended dividend. They do not justify a valuation premium to better operators.

Strongest counter-case. The Norwegian fiscal regime makes the downside shallow. The state absorbs 78% of any cost overrun and any price fall, Var's free cash flow before dividends breaks even at USD 40-45 Brent, and its credit ratings are investment grade. Few cyclical companies have a floor like that.

What would change my view. Var closing the unit-cost and uptime gap to Aker BP; a capital-allocation framework stated in per-share terms; a hedging policy for the krone.

Against the market. The market gives Var the highest own-history valuation percentile in its peer group, as if Var were the best house in the neighbourhood. I rank Var a mid-ranked house in a good neighbourhood. I agree with the market on the fiscal regime and the balance sheet.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Qualitatively the advantages are mostly the basin's (consolidated shelf, high barriers, the state carrying 78% of cost) while Var is a price-taker, third on cost at about USD 11/boe against Aker BP's 7.3-8.8, with an 8-9% base decline, suppliers with the upper hand and Eni controlling a third of the board and 79% of offtake; management allocates capital well but lands operations at the bottom of guidance. Return on invested capital of 12% (74th percentile) and an 81% EBITDA margin (98th) overstate it because the margin becomes about 14% net after tax, free cash flow from 2019-25 was USD 0.47bn against 7.3bn of dividends and predictability is low, though tie-backs at about 35% returns keep new capital above its cost; well above Ithaca's negative post-tax returns, below IMCD's real moat, coherent with the four groups (42, 24, 44, 44).

#4Conservative current guidance; proactivity in keeping sell-side expectations conservative; a track record of fundamental delivery, raising guidance and raising sell-side estimates

Conclusion: Var's guidance is specific and honest, but not conservative on anything that reaches earnings. The company's record of upgrades lies in payouts and ambitions, not in operations.

Evidence. Var's guidance record is consistent: operating guidance is trimmed, and what management sets by decision is raised.

  • Production. 2025 production landed at the bottom of its range. 2026 guidance was cut from 390,000-410,000 to "about 390,000" boe a day, and it still requires about 410,000 in the fourth quarter after 369,000 in the third (the model has 395,000 for the year).
  • Capex. Capital spending runs at the top of its range.
  • Decisions. Management raised the dividend twice in 2026, the long-term production target with each acquisition, and the Neptune synergy target twice.
  • Peers. Var is the exception in a peer group (Aker BP, Harbour, DNO) that guides low and then raises.
  • Disclosure. Guidance is unusually specific on inputs (volumes, unit cost, capex by type, cash tax by quarter, hedges, and a trading update ten days before each result) and silent on EPS, the tax rate and the per-share effect of BlueNord.

Inference. Nothing that produced this pattern has changed, so the pattern is the best forecast for the next 18 months. I expect the first combined 2027 production guide to be centred near 440,000 boe a day. My probabilities for each guidance event are shown below.

The dividend is where guidance can beat our base case, and the reason lies in the payout policy.

The USD 1.45bn of dividends declared for 2026 is 21-22% of post-tax operating cash flow, below the policy band of 25-30% in the peak year; reaching 25% would take another USD 0.2-0.25bn. The 2028 base dividend is about 35% of post-tax operating cash flow, above the band. A band defined "over the cycle" covers both years, and the controlling shareholder's need for cash argues for paying more.

So what. Guidance events will not deliver earnings upgrades. One guidance event can help the shares: the dividend framework on 9 February 2027.

Strongest counter-case. After two years of cuts, management may finally set a production range it can beat. The fourth quarter of 2026 has no planned maintenance turnarounds, output reached 401,000 boe a day in August, and Balder Phase VI is starting. A 2027 range centred at or below 430,000 boe a day would be new behaviour.

What would change my view. A conservative 2027 production range, followed by two quarters delivered in its upper half.

Against the market. The sector story is "guide low and beat, so consensus is a floor". For Var that story holds only through the price deck, never through operations: the visible consensus volume for 2027, up to 445,000 boe a day, is above ours.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Operating guidance has been missed or trimmed two years running (2025 production at the bottom of its range, 2026 cut from 390,000-410,000 to about 390,000 boe a day, unit cost raised from about USD 10 to 11/boe, capex at the top of range, cash flow below consensus four quarters running), and that is what reaches earnings; what management sets by decision (dividend raised twice, Neptune synergies doubled, long-term targets) has gone up. Specific, honest guidance with upgrades only in payouts sits below the Guidance group's 40 because a multi-year record of operating misses weighs heavily, between Hexatronic's weak two-year record and Indutrade's move to mixed delivery.

#5A business model that has pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out/cost control scope and/or reinforcing feedback loops, meaning revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth

Conclusion: Var's business model has high operating leverage, no pricing power and almost no cost scope after tax. The leverage that amplified 2026 now amplifies the decline.

Evidence.

  • Pricing power: none. Var's realised price is the benchmark price plus a small differential, less contract lags when prices rise and plus them when prices fall. In the third quarter of 2026 Var's gas realised USD 18/boe below spot; in the first half of 2027 the same contract structure should realise USD 4-5 above spot. BlueNord arrives with mandatory hedges far below spot (oil near USD 65 a barrel, gas near EUR 31/MWh), which cost about USD 0.2bn of 2027 revenue.
  • Operating leverage: high. About USD 38/boe of cost stands ahead of EBIT (cash cost of about USD 14 and depreciation of about USD 24), and none of it moves with price. A 10% move in price therefore changes EBIT by 16% at 2026 levels and by 21% at the 2028 deck.
  • Cost-out: small after tax. The state takes 78% of every saving through tax. Identifiable gross savings of USD 0.25-0.30bn a year by 2029 reach EPS as only USD 0.02-0.03. The lever that matters is uptime: four points of production efficiency is 15,000 boe a day and USD 0.45/boe off unit cost, with no cost removed.
  • Financial leverage: a drag. The balance sheet is comfortable, but finance costs and hybrid coupons take about USD 0.077 from 2027 EPS. That is 15% of 2027 EPS, more than every cost lever combined. Finance costs are about USD 480m a year now that interest is no longer capitalised, of which about USD 190m is non-cash accretion.
  • Feedback loops: one strong, and reversible. The tax-payment lag moves cash from 2027-28 into 2026 (chart under judgement 2). Hub consolidation makes each tie-back cheaper than the last, but only slowly. The valuation loop is the strong one: Var's high share price was the currency for BlueNord, and the loop reverses if investors doubt the yield.

Inference. The mechanism Richard looks for, revenue growth producing outsized profit growth, is present in full and running in reverse. The commodity price accounts for three-quarters of the fall in EPS; what the company controls accounts for about 1%.

So what. Var's earnings are a geared, unhedged position in the commodity with a company attached. Management cannot bend the 2027-28 EPS path; it can only decide how much to pay out along it.

Strongest counter-case. The gearing is symmetric, and three factors cushion the downside: the state shares 78% of any fall, gas-price indexation lags in Var's favour as prices drop, and the fixed-price share of gas sales limits the effect in the near quarters. If the price deck merely stays flat from here, the leverage stops hurting.

What would change my view. A price path that is flat or rising into 2028; or a decision to sell forward part of the 2027 gas production, which management has said it will not do.

Against the market. I agree with the Street on Var's leverage to price. I differ below EBIT. FactSet's 2027 consensus has pre-tax profit above EBIT (USD 7,122m against 6,875m), which implies net financial income for a company whose finance costs ran at USD 334m a year before it took on BlueNord's debt.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. The structure has very high operating gearing to price (about USD 38/boe of cost ahead of EBIT, none of it moving with price, so a 10% price move changes EBIT by 16-21%, and a marginal barrel earns about USD 44/boe), but no pricing power, almost no cost-out scope after the state takes 78% of every saving, financial leverage that subtracts (finance costs and hybrid coupons take about 15% of 2027 EPS) and a valuation loop that reverses if the yield is doubted. Gearing to a price the company cannot set, now running in reverse (revenue -21%, EPS -56% from 2026 to 2028), places it between Maersk's extreme price gearing (32) and BP's high fixed-cost leverage (50), above the Financial forecasts group's 18 because that group scores the falling forecast path, not the structure.

#6Forecast financials; scope for double digit or higher growth; scope for higher growth/margins than the past over the next four years or so

Conclusion: The forecasts show a level of business well above history and a falling path from 2026, with no scope for double-digit growth and margins no higher than the past at a like-for-like price.

Evidence. The table shows the forecasts of record, with the cash basis beside them.

Inference. The forecasts describe a business that is larger and steadier than before, but no longer growing.

  • Growth from here: none. Revenue falls about 7% a year from 2026 to 2030 and EPS about 20% a year (my arithmetic). There is no double-digit growth on the base deck, nor on the bull deck, where 2027 EPS only matches 2026's.
  • Against the past: a step higher, and secure. Revenue for 2027-30 averages about USD 11.5bn against USD 7.4bn for 2023-25. That is 55% more revenue, on 53% more production, at about the same realised price (USD 74/boe against 73). The forecasts do not lean on prices above pre-shock history, and the volume is already in the run rate or contracted.
  • Margins: unchanged at a like-for-like price (#3).
  • Per share: far less than the volume suggests. 2029 EPS is only 10-30% above 2025's, on 28% more production.
  • Cash: the line that changes character. Free cash flow is positive every year and, once the tax lag clears, about equals distributions at roughly USD 75 Brent.

So what. The model describes a larger, steadier, lower-growth company than the one the market re-rated: its appeal is scale and cash, not earnings growth. Against consensus, our operating lines are higher for 2027 and 2028 while our EPS is 14% and 17% lower (chart under judgement 4; table below). The model's printed net income gap of about -10% includes the hybrid coupons, which the model carries in the tax line; on a like-for-like basis our net income is level with consensus.

Strongest counter-case. The forecasts may be too low: if the 2027 gas curve is delivered (#1), if volume reaches the top of a 440,000 boe a day guide (+USD 0.02 of EPS), or if the three brokers who see 2029 net income rising 23% are right that depreciation falls. The forecasts may equally be too high for the first half of 2027, where about USD 0.5bn of first-quarter revenue above consensus rests on winter gas prices.

What would change my view. First-quarter 2027 realised prices against the deck; the first consolidated depreciation and finance charges, due in late April 2027; evidence of standalone production holding at 385,000-390,000 boe a day through a full year.

Against the market. The market reads 2026 as a new level of earning power, to be defended by the dividend. I read 2026 as the peak of a path whose plateau is about USD 0.32-0.34 of EPS and about USD 1.3-1.4bn of free cash flow a year.

Score: 13, set by the Rater. Falling EPS gives F; the decline is price normalisation from a windfall plus BlueNord dilution, organic in the sense that nothing the company does offsets it, and the bull deck still shows no growth. I place it a little above the floor because the plateau (2029 EPS 10-30% above 2025's) sits above the pre-shock level on 53% more production and margins hold at their like-for-like past, unlike a structural collapse.

#7Scope for forecasts to lead to upgrades to company guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative (investors and sell-side) over the coming 6-12 months

Conclusion: Over the next 6-12 months there is modest scope for upgrades to operating lines, cash flow and the payout, and a higher probability of downgrades to EPS and to in-year volume guidance.

Evidence. Three forces act on consensus EPS, independently of one another.

  1. Mechanical re-basing (judgement 4): downward, near-certain and dated. The BlueNord deal completes around year-end, brokers publish combined-company models with the 9 February results, and Var reports its first consolidated quarter in late April.
  2. Items below EBIT: downward and gradual. Consensus depreciation for 2027 is about USD 0.26bn below ours, although BlueNord's assets enter the accounts at fair value, and consensus finance items look too favourable (#5).
  3. The price deck: two-way, and no longer a tailwind. Eight of the twelve visible broker estimates are dated 21 October, the day before Brent peaked.

Guidance is covered in #4. On the narrative, both the bull and the bear cases are well argued above EBITDA. No covering broker has yet assembled four points: the per-share arithmetic; the true multiple; the fact that 2028 is uncovered on every price path; and the fact that the payout policy leaves room to pay more in February as well as reason to worry later.

Inference. The lines of consensus will part company: EPS is likely to be cut, while revenue and EBITDA are balanced and free cash flow leans up. Free cash flow leans up because, on FactSet's definition, our 2027 free cash flow is about USD 2.3-2.5bn against a consensus of USD 1.45bn. The net breadth of revisions, strongly positive for a year, should fade to neutral around the turn of the year and then turn negative. The 81% rise in 2027 consensus EPS over the last twelve months is finished.

So what. The scope for positive surprise over the next 6-12 months lies in cash and payout, and it comes early. The scope for negative surprise lies in EPS and volume guidance, and it comes later. Almost all the items the narrative has not yet absorbed will hurt the shares when investors notice them.

Strongest counter-case. A cold winter with the gas curve delivered would lift operating estimates by more than the re-basing removes. The 2027 consensus EPS would then hold near USD 0.60, and the February dividend would surprise on the upside. That is the bull path, at 20 in 100, and even on the bull path 2027 EPS is only level with 2026's.

What would change my view. Consensus EPS not falling after BlueNord completes, which would show that brokers are already on the correct basis; the 2028 consensus continuing to rise as it did over the last month (+11%); a 2027 production guide that proves beatable.

Against the market. The mean target price is NOK 56.7, 14% above the share price, yet the share of buy ratings is falling. Analysts have been raising estimates without the conviction to match: the buy share falls as the estimates rise. I think the analysts' next move is to stop raising their estimates. Evidence on what investors, as distinct from analysts, think is thin: a Morgan Stanley conference note (holders like the payout framework and were stress-testing the dividend) and a second-hand account of Norwegian retail investor forums focused on the 10% yield.

Score: 24, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, leans to cuts on the lines that reach earnings (2026 production guide missed 60 in 100, the 2027 guide trimmed 50 against raised 10, unit cost raised 40), with the one likely raise in the dividend framework on 9 February (USD 400m a quarter 60 in 100); consensus EPS, which counts next, should fall mechanically on the per-share re-basing (2027 lower 50 against 20, 2028 lower 65 against 15) and on depreciation and finance items, while free cash flow is more likely raised. With revenue falling, any cut is large against the growth rate; a stale consensus above the correct basis and a narrative that has not yet absorbed the uncovered 2028 make this a net negative scope close to the fourth-set group's 30, just above Xvivo.

#8Currently strong momentum in guidance upgrades, sell-side upgrades, narrative (investors and sell-side), share price technical momentum, and the same for key peers

Conclusion: Technical and estimate momentum are still strong, but they belong to the sector. The momentum specific to Var, in guidance, ratings and relative performance, has already turned down.

Evidence.

  • Sell-side. 2027 consensus EPS and target prices have risen strongly over one, three and six months (chart below). But the share of buy ratings is 47%, down 5 points in a month and 10 points in six months, and the dashboard's sell-side momentum letter is B, down from A a month ago. Var's revision score of 10 is mid-pack in a sector running from 0 to 15.
  • Guidance. Down on operations, up on payout (#4).
  • Narrative. DNB Carnegie moved to Sell on 25 September; the third-quarter miss and guidance cut followed on 21 October.
  • Technical: letter A. The share price is 10.3% above a 200-day average that has risen in each of the last twelve months, relative strength is at the 88th percentile, and the twelve-month return is +63.5%. The price is also 16% below its 52-week high, below its 50-day average (NOK 53.4), and up only 4.9% over three months.
  • Peers. 13 of the 19 sector peers carry a technical A, and every one carries a thematic A. Aker BP has earnings momentum A and technical B; Equinor, DNO and BlueNord have technical A and earnings momentum C.
  • Co-movement. The peer basket explains 74% of Var's daily share-price moves over six months, with a beta of 1.25. Over those six months Var returned 7.8% against 8.9% for the basket, about three points less than its beta implies, and the share of Var's moves that is specific to Var has risen from 19% to 26%.

Inference. Var's momentum is strong, and it is borrowed. The revisions are the sector's, delivered through price decks marked up in late October. The part of the momentum that belongs to Var (ratings, guidance, relative performance since August) has already turned. Estimate momentum is the measure most likely to weaken next, because its inputs pre-date the fall in Brent and the per-share correction.

So what. Momentum still supports the shares today. Of the three pillars that carried the past year (volume growth, a covered dividend and rising estimates), momentum is the last one still standing. Momentum is not a reason to expect the fundamentals to follow.

Strongest counter-case. Price trends persist. A stock above a rising 200-day average, in a sector at full thematic strength, with winter ahead and a dividend decision in February, can stay strong for longer than the fundamentals suggest.

What would change my view. On the downside: a close below the 200-day average (about NOK 45), or Brent under USD 85, the level that removes the reason for holding the sector at all. On the upside: new highs accompanied by rising 2028 estimates.

Against the market. I agree with all three dashboard letters: technical A, sell-side B and valuation F. My difference is one of direction: the sell-side B describes the last three months and flatters the next three.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. Both measures in the top fifth would give A, but parts are negative: guidance was cut on production and unit cost on 21 October, DNB Carnegie moved to Sell and the buy share fell 10 points in six months, and the price is below its 50-day average, 16% off its high and up only 4.9% in three months, so B. I place it in the upper half of the band because 2027 consensus EPS is up 39% over three months (98th percentile), the price is 10% above a rising 200-day average and peers carry technical and thematic A, though the revisions are the sector's price decks, not Var's own.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations: the simplicity of the case and its key drivers; its fragilities, assumptions and requirements; the suddenness, predictability, trackability, prevalence and materiality of risks to the share price, whether justified fundamentally or not; and sector and cyclicality risks, drawing on historical precedents in the sector and industry

Conclusion: The case is simple and unusually trackable but not low-risk, because a wide, externally set range of outcomes meets a peak multiple, a beta of 1.25 and a set of sudden sentiment risks.

Evidence. Simplicity: the case is simple to trace and hard to bank. One external number, the oil and gas price, passes through a short, well-disclosed chain to EBITDA. The last step, from EBITDA to EPS, runs through five items the company does not bridge: post-merger depreciation, finance costs, tax translation, hybrid coupons and share count. As a result, EBITDA was within 1.4% of consensus in each of the last two quarters, while net income was 74% above consensus and then 35% below.

The range of revenue outcomes opens late. Revenue for the next two quarters is close to fixed, and those two quarters make up 39% of the next six quarters' revenue. From the second quarter of 2027 the range widens sharply.

What holds on every price path.

  • EPS does not rise in 2027 and falls in 2028.
  • Distributions exceed free cash flow in 2028.
  • Leverage stays at or below about 1.1x EBITDA, with hybrids counted as debt.
  • USD 3.4-4.5bn of tax on 2026 income is paid in the first half of 2027, two-fifths in the first quarter and three-fifths in the second. The second quarter of 2027 is therefore the quarter in which free cash flow before the dividend is roughly nil (my arithmetic).
  • Consensus EPS is re-based.

The risks, by character.

Precedents: a sharp, short cash trough that the equity market prices early. After the 2022 peak Var's revenue, EBIT and free cash flow fell sharply within a year, and the shares reached 4.8x forward earnings on an 18% yield in early 2023 (tiles below). Equinor fell about 30% within seven months. In 2014 Statoil stood at 12.2x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 8.9x, as Brent turned. In 2014 and 2018 share prices fell months before estimates did. The companies that held up had low costs and low leverage (Aker BP, Lundin) or hedges (Harbour, BlueNord). Var has the low leverage, but not the low cost, and it has no hedges.

Inference. The risk of being wrong about the company is small, because the base case needs only strengths Var has already shown. The risk of being wrong about one external price is large, and an investor takes that risk through the highest multiple in the peer group. In the precedents the balance sheet survives the cash trough, so the downside is a de-rating, not an impairment.

So what. With a risk profile like Var's, position sizing and timing matter as much as direction. The case can be tested on known dates (the late-January trading update, 9 February, end-March gas storage and the late-April first consolidated quarter). That is a real advantage: apart from the commodity price, little of what decides the case will arrive unannounced.

Strongest counter-case. Few cyclical companies come with Var's shock absorbers: a 78% tax shield, USD 7.5bn of liquidity, contract lags that pay in a falling market, and disclosure good enough to know a quarter's EBITDA before it is reported.

What would change my view. A lower entry multiple, which would remove most of the sentiment risk; or currency and gas hedging, which would narrow the range of outcomes.

Against the market. Holders treat the stock as a 10% yield with an energy hedge attached: a low-risk income case. I see a simple, well-tracked, high-variance case. Both descriptions are true of Var's cash flows; only the second is true of its share price.

Score: 20, set by the Rater. The memo's 2027 EPS range runs from USD 0.27 to 0.81 around 0.51 (about -47% to +59%), set by one external price with no hedges, five unbridged items between EBITDA and EPS, a beta of 1.25 to the sector on the cohort's richest multiple, and sudden risks (commodity normalisation, sector de-rating below USD 85 Brent, an unsignalled Eni placing, outages at hubs carrying 40% of output, a dated fiscal review). The 78% tax shield, 0.3x leverage, USD 7.5bn of liquidity and unusually trackable, dated disclosure keep it off the bottom (no balance-sheet event on any path), so it sits just above Ithaca's comparable commodity-and-tax case, between the two Risks groups (24 and 40) but nearer the first because the share-price cone, not the operating one, is wide.

#10An assessment of where the stock plausibly is in its lifecycle (based on current momentum, scope for upgrades, risk factors): bottoming, turning up, thesis broadening, reinforcing, stalling or collapsing

Conclusion: The stock is at the end of its Reinforcing phase and beginning to stall, with a further three months of supportive news plausible before the stall shows in the numbers.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the Reinforcing phase, and on trailing evidence that placement is right: a 64% rise over the year, a rising 200-day average and twelve months of upgrades. But each of the three drivers of the Reinforcing phase has run its course.

  • The volume doubling is complete: year-on-year production growth went from +51% in the first quarter of 2026 to zero in the third.
  • 2026 is the first year in which free cash flow covers the dividend.
  • The estimate upgrades are ending (#7).

The first signs of the next phase are already visible: a guidance cut, an earnings miss, a broker downgrade on valuation, ratings drifting lower while targets rise, and Var beginning to lag its own sector.

Inference. I place the stock at the end of Reinforcing, tipping into Stalling, with the price trend not yet confirming the shift. The stock is not Collapsing: no path in the range of outcomes leads to a forced balance-sheet event, and the dividend holds on the base deck. I expect the sequence below.

So what. In a Stalling phase forecasts are less certain, and the market pays a lower multiple than at peak delivery. This is the bridge to #11: the guideline multiple is set for the phase the stock is leaving.

Strongest counter-case. A stock can re-enter Reinforcing if its driver renews. If gas stays short through 2027, the 2028 estimates (up 11% in the last month) keep rising, the dividend is raised, and the Reinforcing phase extends by a year.

What would change my view. Outer-year consensus still rising after the per-share correction; new share-price highs on delivered 2027 guidance. In the other direction, a break of the 200-day average together with a cut to the 2027 production guide would signal that Stalling has arrived early.

Against the market. Target prices and the technical letter say Reinforcing; the drift in ratings says analysts already sense Stalling. I side with the ratings.

Score: 28, set by the Rater. The computed Reinforcing is right only on trailing evidence: the volume doubling is complete (production growth from +51% to zero), the upgrades are ending, and the first signs of Stalling are in (guidance cut, earnings miss, a valuation downgrade, ratings drifting lower, Var lagging its sector), with revenue below the prior year in every quarter from Q2 2027 and the input force reversing. I agree with the memo's end of Reinforcing tipping into Stalling, with about three months of supportive news first; it is not Collapsing because the dividend holds and there is no balance-sheet path, so it sits just below Zegona's Stalling and well above Judges' collapse.

#11The fair multiple (higher in historical range for stock in peak delivery phases; lower for stalling or turning up, where forecasts are more uncertain)

Conclusion: In my view the guideline 9.41x is a fair central multiple: generous for a stalling stock on its own history, but justified by a stronger company and a re-rated sector. The dividend's credibility decides whether the shares rest nearer 8x or 12x.

Evidence. The guideline fair multiple is 9.41x two-year-forward earnings: the 90th percentile of the stock's own history, the level set for a Reinforcing phase. Today's multiple is 14.0x on the model's EPS, 12.8x on the dashboard's consensus basis and 11.5x on FactSet's (6 November). The three figures differ because of the EPS basis and the date, not because of a different view of the price. The stock's own median is 6.9x and its 75th percentile 8.1x.

Inference: my view of the guideline. I think 9.41x is a fair central figure. Five lenses give different answers, and the arguments in each direction roughly cancel.

  • Phase: 9.41x is too high. The stock is leaving Reinforcing. By the guideline's own logic a stalling stock sits lower in its range, and the middle of the range is 6.9-8.1x.
  • History: 9.41x is too low. The "ten-year" history covers only 56 months, all since the February 2022 listing: the build-out years, when free cash flow was negative and the dividend was borrowed. The company is now twice the size, a third as levered and able to fund its distributions over a cycle. That argues for the top of the old range, which is where 9.41x sits.
  • Sector: 9.41x is about right. The median peer trades at the 78th percentile of its own history. Had Var re-rated only that far, its multiple would be about 9.4x. The guideline therefore removes Var's own excess (about 2.1 turns) and leaves the sector's re-rating (about 2.6 turns) in place. A reader who expects the sector's re-rating to fade too should use about 8x.
  • Yield: 9.41x is low, unless the dividend is doubted. At 9.41x the shares would stand near NOK 30, where the USD 0.51 dividend yields 16%. A held, believed dividend at a 12-14% yield implies 11-13x. A dividend cut to the policy level, at a 12% yield, implies NOK 27-33, close to the guideline. So the guideline is the right multiple if the dividend is cut or disbelieved, and one to three turns too low if the dividend is believed. History leans towards doubt: through the build-out years, when free cash flow did not cover the payout, the market kept this stock on a yield in the teens (my arithmetic from the price history and dividends). 2028 is again a year without cover, though with less than half the leverage.
  • Cash: 9.41x is about right. At the guideline price, steady-state free cash flow after hybrid coupons is a 14.5-15% yield (my arithmetic: USD 1.25-1.31bn over 2,744.8m shares, against a share price of USD 3.13). Today the free cash flow yield is about 9%. For comparison, Bernstein's work of March 2026 had Aker BP's free cash flow yield rising to about 14% in 2027 as its capex falls. A mid-teens cash yield is what a buyer of a no-growth producer can reasonably ask.

One caution on the P/E measure itself. Depreciation (about USD 3.6bn) exceeds capital spending (about USD 3.0-3.2bn), so in steady state free cash flow runs about 40% above net income. A P/E therefore undervalues Var's cash. But the excess is partly a return of capital from a depleting base, with USD 5.3bn of abandonment obligations behind it, so I would not adjust the multiple for it.

So what. I would use 9.41x as the centre of an 8x to 12x range, and treat the credibility of the 2028 dividend as what decides where in that range the stock rests.

Strongest counter-case. The bears argue that a depleting, no-growth, commodity-priced earnings stream deserves its own median multiple, about 7x. The bulls cite Morgan Stanley's dividend discount model, which at a 9% cost of equity supports NOK 56, about today's multiple.

What would change my view. The language of the 9 February dividend framework (a dividend base stated for 2027-28 would move me up the range); a shift in the policy rate or in the cost of equity for dividend stocks; a sector de-rating (which would move me down the range).

Against the market. The market pays 14x, and broker targets assume that this multiple, or a higher price deck, persists. In my view the market prices the 2026 yield as permanent, while the guideline prices it as doubtful; the truth likely lies between the two, and nearer the guideline.

Score: 28, set by the Rater. On the raw readings dear on one and cheap on the other gives C, but the peer cheapness is not real: consensus EPS is overstated by share count and hybrid coupons, so the true multiple is 14.0x not 12.8x, which puts Var at about 1.19x the cohort, only about 8% below its norm, and a stock tipping into Stalling deserves less than its peak history, so I move the letter to D. Placed low in the band because measure 1 is at the very top of its range and today's 14.0x sits about 50% above the memo's fair 9.41x and twice the stock's 6.9x median.

#12Total shareholder return, via the DuPont framework (split into earnings growth, the change in the multiple, and dividends and other cash returns); expressed over the next 6-18 months and the next three years

Conclusion: The model's return is -26% to March 2028 and -20% to September 2029, because a 33% fall in the multiple and a 10-16% fall in forward earnings outweigh a dividend of about 10% a year. Even with no de-rating, the 18-month return is only about 3%.

Evidence. The model's return at the guideline multiple is negative at both horizons.

-19.9%annualised, to 31 March 2028
NOK 36.48value per share including dividends, March 2028
-7.6%annualised, to 30 September 2029
NOK 39.45value per share including dividends, September 2029

Inference: what drives each part of the return.

  • Dividends are the only positive leg, the only leg the company controls, and the most probable: about USD 0.69 a share to March 2028. The dividend leg rests on the dividend base being held, which I put at about 85 in 100 over the period.
  • The multiple is the largest leg. It falls from 14.0x to 9.41x, taken in full by the 18-month column and held thereafter. The multiple is a judgement about spring 2028, when the uncovered year is under way and the market decides whether to believe the dividend.
  • Earnings fall because two-year-forward EPS moves from about USD 0.37 today to 0.33 in March 2028 and 0.31 in September 2029. Three things drive the fall: the deck settling at Brent USD 72-73 and TTF EUR 30-32/MWh, a slowly declining production plateau (428,000 to 417,000 boe a day), and fixed finance costs and coupons.
  • The three-year return looks better than the 18-month return because the de-rating is taken only once. After the de-rating, at about NOK 30, the stock would earn its dividend yield less a slow erosion in earnings.

The return under other assumptions (my arithmetic on the model's split). With no de-rating, the 18-month return is about +3%, and with a believed dividend it is -17% to -5% (judgement 3 and #11). The bull path gives roughly +15%: prices near late-2026 levels through 2027 would leave the shares about where they are, on a multiple and a set of doubts much like today's, plus the dividends. The bear path gives about -35%, with the shares near NOK 26 after a dividend cut.

My indicative weights are 20 in 100 for the bull path, 50 for the base path (spanning the guideline and believed-dividend outcomes) and 30 for the bear path. Together they give a probability-weighted return of about -15% to March 2028, with roughly one chance in five of a positive result. These are rough figures to show the skew; the model's figures are the figures of record.

Over the next six months I expect the return to be better than the 18-month figure implies, because the supportive events come first (#7) and the de-rating needs the 2028 cash gap to come into view.

So what. The return is negative because the buyer pays today's peak multiple on falling earnings, and the dividend is not large enough to offset both. The arithmetic turns at a lower price. The guideline value including dividends is NOK 36.5 at March 2028, so an entry near NOK 32-33 would return 10-15% over the period, with a held dividend yielding about 15% while the investor waits.

NOK 32-33the entry price at which the return to March 2028 turns to +10-15%, with a held dividend yielding about 15% while the investor waits

Strongest counter-case. The Street's case is a target price of NOK 56.7 which, with the dividend, gives a 12-month return of about 24%. That case requires the multiple to hold at the top of its history through the re-basing of EPS, or a long-run price deck well above ours; break-even alone needs about USD 12.5/boe more (judgement 3).

What would change my view. A believed dividend base for 2027-28, which would move the base outcome towards -10%; a structurally higher price deck; a lower entry price.

Against the market. The gap between the Street's +24% and the model's negative return is almost entirely the multiple and the per-share basis, not the operating forecast. The next two quarters of consensus mechanics, not the next two quarters of trading, will therefore start to settle the disagreement.

Score: 11, set by the Rater. A loss gives F, and -15% maps to about 12; the three-year check confirms it, and even with no de-rating the 18-month return is only about +3% because the dividend merely offsets falling earnings. I move it down one for the fat lower tail (bear at about -35% with a 30 in 100 weight, only one chance in five of a positive result), though the near six months should be better than the 18-month figure.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Var Energi is a sound business priced as an exceptional one. The basin is protected, the state shares the costs, the balance sheet is the strongest it has been and the chief executive allocates capital well. The barrel earns what it always did. What the shares offer at NOK 49.6 is narrower: a geared, unhedged position in oil and European gas at the peak of a supply shock, on the highest multiple in the peer group. EPS falls for two years on every price path, and the dividend is safe on the base deck but uncovered in 2028 on every path.

The situation Richard looks for is not here today. Fundamental outcomes and the odds of upgrades are not skewed to the positive. The skew in EPS revisions is negative for mechanical reasons, guidance is not conservative, and the multiple has room to fall and little room to rise. What is positively skewed is narrower and nearer: cash flow in 2027, the February dividend decision and the BlueNord synergies.

The case has a clear sequence. Three months of mostly supportive, dated news come first. From spring 2027 come the re-based EPS line, falling year-on-year revenue and the largest tax payment, and by early 2028 the uncovered year.

Almost all of the case arrives on known dates, so it can be watched with unusual precision and revisited on evidence. Three triggers would make Var attractive: a share price in the low-to-mid NOK 30s; a gas market that stays short through the 2027 storage refill; or a management team that, for once, sets a production range and then beats it.

The four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 20, set by the Rater. The external input force is a windfall price reversing (topic 1 at 20) and the internal forces are funded but per-share neutral and offset by operating slippage (topic 2 at 47), so nothing offsets the reversal, and the financial output confirms it: EPS falls about 20% a year from the 2026 peak with no growth on any price path (topic 6, F). This is clear net negative change reaching profits surely, worse than Shell's or Indus's reversing windfall because the fall is steeper, but short of Maersk's overwhelming contracted blow since profits settle on a plateau above the pre-shock past.

Foundations' Robustness: 42, set by the Rater. A protected basin where the state carries 78% of costs and price falls, an investment-grade balance sheet, free-cash-flow breakeven before dividends at USD 40-45 Brent and returns above the cost of capital make the foundations safe, but Var is a price-taker, third on cost, with a fast-declining base, minimal ordinary equity and Eni control (topic 3 at 40), and its operating delivery against guidance has been at or below the bottom for two years (topic 4 at 36). A strong balance sheet offset by an ordinary moat and a poor recent delivery record sits below typical, a little below the memo's C.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 10, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits no Target Setup and is the inverse of the nearest one, CfC in a quality cyclical at trough-on-trough: it is a cyclical at peak earnings with the input force turning, a windfall at the point the setup would sell. Its serial-acquirer and corporate-change features produce no step-up in earnings per share and today's operating problems blur even those, so it sits with Maersk's windfall at the 10 level, a touch above because the plateau and payout are real.

Case Riskiness: 24, set by the Rater. The case is simple, trackable on known dates and safe at the balance sheet on every path, which lifts it a little above topic 9's 20, but it is a single-driver case whose 2027 EPS range runs about -47% to +59% on one unhedged external price, taken through the cohort's peak multiple with a beta of 1.25 and sudden sentiment risks (sector de-rating, an Eni placing), so the main risk is a de-rating of 25-45%. A simple single-driver case that does not offset a range wider than a quarter either way sits in the 25 band, matching the memo's D.

End notes

How to read the numbers

  • The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). EPS follows the company's own definition: after the coupons on its hybrid bonds, and on 2,744.8m shares from the BlueNord completion expected around year-end 2026. Consensus is the FactSet median at 11 November 2026; consensus EPS sits on a different per-share basis, and the difference matters (judgement 4 in #0).
  • For dividend cover I use free cash flow on the cash basis, with tax counted when it is paid. The model's "equity free cash flow" counts tax when it is charged, which smooths the years: right for leverage, wrong for cover.
  • "My arithmetic" marks figures I derive here from the files' numbers.
  • I change no forecast input. The base price deck is at or just below spot for the next two quarters and in the middle of the brokers' decks for 2027, and the per-share corrections made after the previous round of work are already in the model. Where I differ from the earlier work is in the weights around the base case and in how I read the fair multiple.
  • Abbreviations: boe is barrels of oil equivalent; TTF is the Dutch Title Transfer Facility gas price; LNG is liquefied natural gas; mmbtu is million British thermal units.

One check for the Financial Analyst

Between the model's two return columns, which are 18 months apart, the dividend leg grows by 9.8 points, exactly one year's dividend of USD 0.51. On calendar timing a further two or three quarterly payments would be received by September 2029, worth 5-7 points (my inference from the published split; I have not seen the sheet). If so, the three-year return is nearer -14% than -20.5%. The conclusion does not change.

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • FY2025 earnings per share: 0.31 on the brokers' basis against 0.14 on our model's basis (+114.5%).
  • Consensus net income for FY2026 is 2,060.00, +471.0% against 360.80 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +80.4%.
  • Consensus earnings per share for FY2026 is 0.79, +448.6% against 0.14 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +80.4%.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Amortisation of acquired intangibles over the last twelve months: -0.2 before tax (-0.00 per share); our model's FY2025 history does not exclude it (its EBITA equals EBIT). Brokers' adjusted figures often exclude it.
  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
